inventory.interpretation_note: The raw archive is much larger than the interpretation surface that a reader can use directly. The dashboard therefore shows only the comparisons that answer a question clearly, while the underlying tables and files remain available for audit. The latest update also reflects the fact that the published repository now reproduces the full canonical suite from a fresh clone on Falcon.

reading_guide.title: Comparability first
reading_guide.body: Direct clean rows, posterior framework rows, posterior decision rules, hybrid initializers, and active-sequential rows form separate result spaces. Each chart states its own comparison class.

reading_guide.title: Performance versus speedup
reading_guide.body: Performance improvements refer to elapsed time, train time, startup cost, and completed-run throughput. Speedup refers to a ratio against a baseline. The dashboard keeps those quantities separate.

reading_guide.title: Primary versus supporting evidence
reading_guide.body: The Hodgkin-Huxley fixed-task comparison is the empirical center. Benchmark parity, execution studies, and execution-path optimizations support or bound that comparison.

reading_guide.title: Fresh full rerun closure
reading_guide.body: The latest published head completed the full canonical suite from a fresh Falcon clone. That closure matters most for execution, framework, posterior-rule, and surrogate claims, because it turns earlier partial or targeted checks into one end-to-end reproducibility result.

threads.title: Benchmark Parity and Split Integrity
threads.intro: These studies checked whether the inherited FitzHugh-Nagumo baseline remained statistically stable, and whether the archived split behavior remained scientifically interpretable.
threads.how_to_read: Read the metric-delta chart as a bounded difference against the archived benchmark mean, then read the ANOVA chart as a check that node count did not materially change predictive quality.
threads.main_conclusion: The baseline remained statistically close to the archived benchmark, while runtime changed more than predictive quality. The fresh full clean rerun did not change that conclusion, and the split issue still remains an interpretation boundary rather than a moving target.

charts.title: Benchmark deltas against the archived FitzHugh-Nagumo reference
charts.subtitle: Positive values indicate the multi-seed rerun mean was above the archived benchmark value.
notes: The MSE offset is real, but it remains inside the reproduced multi-seed variation envelope.
The R2 shift is very small, which is why the parity conclusion remained positive.

charts.title: Node-count effect test on parity metrics
charts.subtitle: Higher p-values indicate weaker evidence that node count changed model quality.
notes: These p-values support the claim that the benchmark parity result is stable across the tested node counts.
The benchmark study anchors the later systems claims, while remaining supporting evidence rather than a main objective.

threads.title: Execution Configuration and Run Policy
threads.intro: These studies determined which execution setting best supports broad comparative sweeps while keeping the task fixed.
threads.how_to_read: The throughput chart answers the run-policy question. The train-time chart answers a narrower question, namely whether tuned 2-node and 4-node lanes improved inside their own lane, which is different from asking whether multi-node scaling beat the best single-node policy.
threads.main_conclusion: Throughput-first grouped single-node execution remained the default within a fixed workload, while the final runner now also exploits the full 4-node allocation by running independent steps in resource-aware cohorts. Tuned 2-node and 4-node paths improved their own lane materially, but they did not overturn the broad-sweep single-node policy.

cards.title: Fresh full-run scheduler closure
cards.body: The published runner now launches independent 1-node, 2-node, posterior, framework, and surrogate steps concurrently when their node demands do not overlap, while giving each distributed step its own rendezvous port and its own cache roots when needed. The fresh full clean rerun cleared the execution-policy batch and the later overlapping single-node batches under that contract.

charts.title: Completed runs per hour, grouped 1-node versus selected 4-node latency path
charts.subtitle: Higher is better. The current Hodgkin-Huxley workload used the right-hand comparison.
notes: On the current Hodgkin-Huxley task, grouped single-node execution improved completed-run throughput by 85.5%.
This chart establishes single-node execution as the broad default, while 4-node latency remains useful for targeted reference runs.

charts.title: Train-time reduction inside the tuned multi-node lane
charts.subtitle: These percentages compare the tuned `R1_accum2_nosync` lane against the earlier node-matched baseline.
notes: These are node-local improvements rather than broad run-policy wins.
This is why performance and speedup should not be conflated in the dashboard text.

charts.title: Final grouped single-node factorization improvement
charts.subtitle: The `factor_s5` path was the last single-node cleanup before the broad default was closed.
notes: This was a small but clean single-node improvement that preserved quality.
Once this path existed, the broad-default case for 4-node execution weakened further.

threads.title: Primary Direct Fixed-Task Comparison
threads.intro: This is the empirical center of the work. The current clean direct frontier is taken from the homogeneous A30 rerun package, which displaced the older mixed closure endpoint.
threads.how_to_read: Read the accuracy chart as the clean direct comparison within the direct-estimation class, and read the runtime chart separately, because runtime and accuracy answer different questions.
threads.main_conclusion: The direct clean winner is tuned Extra Trees, the robust direct representative is tuned k-nearest neighbors, and the best surviving neural direct row is still materially behind both in the final clean rerun.

cards.title: Latest clean direct frontier
cards.body: In the fresh full clean rerun, `extra_trees_500_depth20` reached a clean MAE of 495.69, `knn_k11` reached 502.44, and the surviving neural direct row reached 913.42. That leaves kNN only 1.36% above the tuned tree on clean MAE, while the neural direct row remains 84.27% above the tuned tree.

charts.title: Clean direct MAE by family representative
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. These rows share one direct-estimation comparison class.
notes: The clean gap from the best neural direct row to the direct winner is 43.1% on MAE.
The clean gap between the direct winner and the robust kNN representative is only 0.34%.

charts.title: Representative runtime by direct family
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. Runtime is a cost measure, so it should be read separately from MAE.
notes: The direct clean winner was also much cheaper than the best surviving neural row.
The kNN representative remained the lowest-runtime direct contender while preserving near-winner clean accuracy.

threads.title: Posterior-Oriented and Representation Follow-Up
threads.intro: These studies broadened the executable comparison through richer observations, stronger posterior families, and later aligned framework rows.
threads.how_to_read: The posterior chart stays inside the posterior-oriented result space. The gain chart identifies which interventions materially improved that space.
threads.main_conclusion: The fresh clean rerun keeps the posterior story but sharpens its ranking. BayesFlow meanstd with a posterior-median rule is now the best posterior MAE row, BayesFlow mean prediction is the best posterior MSE and R2 row, and NPSE median improves over the FMPE extension median in the later extension block.

cards.title: Latest posterior snapshot
cards.body: The clean posterior decision-rule table from the fresh full rerun places `bayesflow_meanstd` median first at MAE 583.42, `bayesflow_meanstd` mean first at MSE 1.784e6 with R2 0.630, `npse_extension` median at MAE 861.43, and `fmpe_extension` median at MAE 1059.11. The older claim that FMPE was the strongest clean posterior family no longer holds under the final published run.

charts.title: Posterior-oriented clean MAE by representative
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. These rows remain inside the posterior-oriented result space.
notes: The BayesFlow median row is the best comparable posterior decision rule by MAE.
FMPE is still the clean posterior-family winner in the checkpoint-2 SBI block.
NPSE stayed slower and weaker than FMPE on the primary point metrics.

charts.title: Posterior-oriented intervention gains
charts.subtitle: Positive values are improvements against the reference named in each label. The combined-corruption row is intentionally negative.
categories: BayesFlow median versus framework MAE gain
notes: The richer observation space mattered before later family expansion.
The combined-corruption negative bar is a guardrail, because that branch damaged clean behavior too severely for promotion.

charts.title: Posterior-oriented runtime by representative
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. This chart reports performance cost rather than predictive quality.
notes: BayesFlow meanstd is the fastest aligned framework row among the promoted posterior-oriented representatives.
The MAE-optimal posterior decision rule is much slower than the aligned framework row, which is why the dashboard keeps accuracy and runtime in separate charts.

threads.title: Shift Robustness and Noise Sensitivity
threads.intro: These studies asked whether the clean winners survived perturbations, and whether shift-specific retraining changed the representative set.
threads.how_to_read: The first chart shows the clean-to-shift-specific posterior interventions. The second chart shows where the robust direct representative gains its practical value.
threads.main_conclusion: Robustness is plural. The fresh clean rerun still says that matched posterior repairs help within their own shift, while the robust direct representative under additive noise is kNN rather than the clean tuned tree.

cards.title: Latest robustness check
cards.body: At additive noise 0.20, `knn_k11` reduced MAE from 916.00 to 510.65 relative to the tuned tree, which is a 44.25% improvement. Inside the posterior family, the drift-specific SNPE retraining row reduced mean-rule MAE from 1135.05 on the clean raw-plus-FFT-plus-summary reference to 1078.92, while the matched mask row reduced it to 1123.65.

charts.title: Shift-specific posterior improvement relative to the clean-trained feature-aware SNPE reference
charts.subtitle: Positive values indicate MAE improvement. The combined-corruption row shows why a single universal corruption-aware model was not promoted.
notes: The positive bars justify shift-specific promoted robustness paths.
The negative combined-corruption bar shows why one pooled robust-SNPE winner would have been misleading.

charts.title: kNN MAE improvement over the tuned tree under additive noise
charts.subtitle: Positive values indicate that kNN reduced MAE relative to `extra_trees_500_depth20` at that noise level.
notes: The direct clean winner and the direct robust winner are different, which is why the dashboard keeps them separate at the top.
The improvement stays material even at the heaviest tested additive noise level.

threads.title: Later Executable Extensions
threads.intro: These studies reduced missed-family risk through aligned framework runs, posterior decision rules, active-sequential ladders, and hybrid initializer rows.
threads.how_to_read: These charts stay inside their own extension class. They broaden coverage within the executable method space.
threads.main_conclusion: The extension surface is now reproducibly executable from a fresh full clean run. In the active-sequential lane, disagreement and Wasserstein are effectively tied on the primary error metric, while ASNPE remains weaker on that same metric even though it closes with a coherent posterior.

charts.title: Active-sequential error metric by representative policy
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. This chart stays inside the active-sequential class.
notes: Disagreement is the lowest row on mean absolute log10 parameter error, but Wasserstein is only 0.31% worse on that metric.
ASNPE now finishes cleanly in the fresh full rerun, but its mean absolute log10 parameter error remains 33.28% above the best active-sequential policy.

charts.title: Active-sequential runtime by representative policy
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. The runtime gap is part of why these rows stayed in their own extension section.
notes: The three active-sequential policies now sit in the same runtime band, roughly 64 seconds, in the fresh clean run.
ASNPE is no longer a runtime outlier, but it is still not competitive on the active-sequential error metric.

cards.title: Wasserstein and disagreement after the clean rerun
cards.body: The final active-sequential summary puts disagreement at mean absolute log10 parameter error 0.74196 and Wasserstein at 0.74426, while Wasserstein retains the explicit distributional interpretation of projected 1-Wasserstein disagreement across posterior predictive draws. The practical difference between those two policies is therefore small in accuracy terms, and the choice between them is now mostly interpretive rather than operational.

threads.title: Execution-Path Optimizations
threads.intro: These studies optimized startup behavior inside the extracted-data Hodgkin-Huxley execution path. They mattered operationally, while the scientific frontier remained unchanged.
threads.how_to_read: The cache charts measure startup reduction inside the execution path. The explanation cards clarify why the branch stayed secondary, even though the later mmap-backed canaries were strong.
threads.main_conclusion: Feature-scale caching reduced preprocessing materially, the mmap-backed split-array cache removed almost all startup overhead in the successful canaries, and the final fresh clean run also confirmed that cache locking and step-local cache isolation are sufficient for concurrent cohorts. The branch is therefore no longer only a canary proof, because it now supports the published concurrent full runner directly.

charts.title: Feature-scale cache preprocessing reduction
charts.subtitle: Positive values indicate preprocessing time reduction relative to the eager path.
notes: This optimization attacked a measured startup bottleneck while preserving the eager hot loop.
That is why feature-scale cache became the extracted-data default before split-array caching did.

charts.title: Split-array mmap startup reduction after the proof chain
charts.subtitle: Positive values indicate data-load reduction against the completed R4 medians for the same families.
notes: The first split-array canary failed badly, which is why the branch was initially kept experimental.
After the mmap-backed reload fix, the branch cleared both the dedicated launcher proof and a broader ordinary-launcher proof, so the remaining question became marginal value rather than correctness.

cards.title: Why it was not tested as a full campaign
cards.body: The branch ultimately addressed startup overhead inside one extracted-data execution path. By the time the later proofs succeeded, the main systems question had already been answered by the throughput-first single-node policy, and the model-frontier question had already moved into family comparison, representation, and robustness work. The split-array branch was therefore tested enough to establish viability, while a full factorial expansion would have consumed effort without changing the main scientific claims.

cards.title: What was actually proved
cards.body: The later proof chain established that the split-array cache could be prewarmed, launched through its ordinary canary package, exercised through an older ordinary HH launcher, protected by explicit cache-file locking, and isolated per parallel cohort when contention risk existed. That is the execution-path contract which survived the final fresh full clean rerun.
